`e2e/specs/56-list-grid.e2e.ts` has an intermittent failure on CI (desktop, `decorations` group).

The case is `puts space-indented levels on the grid whatever the space count` (around line 513). The failing assertion is:

    expect(row.markerX).toBeCloseTo(row.column, 1);

Observed on GitHub Actions run 34001303005 (job `desktop (decorations)`, commit 893c4c5 of branch `feat/backlinks-controls`): `Expected: 0, Received: 14.88`. So the row's marker sat roughly one marker-gutter to the right of the depth-0 column instead of on it.

Context that narrows it:
- The whole `decorations` group passes locally on macOS (8/8 spec files, 30 cases in 56-list-grid) at that same commit.
- It also passed on CI on the immediately preceding runs of the same branch, so it is not a new persistent break.
- The branch's only stylesheet changes at that point were all scoped under `.to-backlinks*` (the backlinks footer's own controls), so they cannot reach `.cm-line` list-grid decorations. The failure is very unlikely to be caused by that branch.

The case loops over three indent styles (`'  '`, `'   '`, `'\t'`) and rebuilds the note each time, so the first thing worth establishing is which iteration failed and whether the measurement ran before the layout settled — 14.88 is suspiciously close to one gutter, which suggests the marker was measured while the row was still being decorated, or that Obsidian's own indent rendering had not yet resolved.

Goal: reproduce it (running the group repeatedly, or under load / with more parallel instances, is the likely route since CI is slower than a dev machine), find the actual cause, and fix either the timing of the measurement or the underlying decoration if it is real. Read `docs/research/` notes on decorations and the list grid before changing anything — several mechanisms there were chosen by measurement and the comments record why.

## context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

- ponytail: Forces the laziest solution that actually works, simplest, shortest, most minimal. Channels a senior dev who has seen everything: question whether the task needs to exist at all (YAGNI), reach for the standard library before custom code, native platform features before dependencies, one line before fifty. Supports intensity levels: lite, full (default), ultra. Use on ANY coding task: writing, adding, refactoring, fixing, reviewing, or designing code, and choosing libraries or dependencies. Also use whenever the user says "ponytail", "be lazy", "lazy mode", "simplest solution", "minimal solution", "yagni", "do less", or "shortest path", or complains about over-engineering, bloat, boilerplate, or unnecessary dependencies. body {
  /* The outline unit: one tree level's worth of horizontal distance, and the
   * only number any layer may derive a column from. Declared rather than left
   * to `var(--to-decor-unit)` fallbacks scattered through the rules and the JS,
   * because it also feeds Obsidian's own `--list-indent`
   * (lists-on-the-outline-grid) — two literals that must agree is exactly the
   * shape this layer has been bitten by before. A snippet can retune it, and
   * every kind moves together.
   *
   * `rem`, never `em`: a custom property resolves where it is USED, so an `em`
   * unit would inflate on a heading's larger font — the Experiment 1 bug. That
   * matters doubly here, since Obsidian's own `--list-indent` IS `em` based and
   * this value replaces it inside outline mode.
   *
   * Declared on `body` rather than on `.cm-content` so the backlinks footer,
   * which is not made of `.cm-line`s, reads the same one. The `--list-indent`
   * bridge that consumes it stays gated on `.to-decor-list`, so outline mode
   * off is still untouched.
   *
   * Overriding THIS declaration is the supported way to retune the outline's
   * width: every column on every surface is derived from it, so a snippet
   * setting it on `body` moves the whole grid and nothing is left behind. That
   * only holds while nothing restates the value — no rule's `var()` fallback,
   * and nothing in JS (see `UNIT_EXPR`). */
  --to-decor-unit: 1.75rem;

  --to-guide-color: color-mix(in srgb, var(--text-faint) 60%, transparent);
  --to-decor-accent: var(--text-accent);

  /* Same width as an unaccented guide, so an accent is purely a change of
   * colour: the line does not thicken as the caret moves into a subtree, and an
   * accented guide sits on exactly the columns and weight the unaccented one
   * did. A heavier value reads as emphasis-by-weight and makes the accented
   * column visibly jump; retune with a snippet if that is wanted. */
  --to-trail-width: 1px;
}

/*
 * `--to-marker-gutter` (Experiment 5a, see
 * docs/research/10-experiment-5-block-markers.md): an additive reservation for
 * a per-kind block marker icon, on top of the existing depth-based
 * indentation. Its VALUE is derived from the marks it has to hold rather than
 * chosen (chrome-tokens.ts, docs/research/21-marker-text-gap.md), so no rule
 * here may restate it — a literal copy goes stale the first time that
 * derivation is re-run. Applies to every non-list-item line (block and
 * atom alike) — list items reserve nothing, since they keep their fully
 * native marker untouched. `rem`, never `em`, same reasoning as
 * `--to-decor-unit` above. Explicitly set per-line by `lineDecoration()`
 * (decorations.ts) — this rule's own fallback (`0px`) only matters before
 * that JS has run at all; it is never the value actually in effect.
 * `position: relative` gives the marker icon
 * (a real, absolutely-positioned DOM child, not a pseudo-element — the
 * whole reason Experiment 5a doesn't need to fight over `::before`/
 * `::after` with the guide or blockquote's native bar) a containing block
 * matching this line's own box.
 */
/* Two surfaces, one rule. The backlinks footer's rows are not `.cm-line`s and
 * are not children of `.cm-content`, but they carry the same class and the same
 * custom properties (`chrome-line.ts`), so they take the same layout from the
 * same declarations rather than from a parallel set that drifts. */
.markdown-source-view.mod-cm6 .cm-content > .cm-line.to-decor-block,
.to-backlinks-row.to-decor-block {
  position: relative;
  padding-left: calc(
    var(--to-depth, 0) * var(--to-decor-unit) + var(--to-marker-gutter, 0px)
  ) !important;
  /* Headings/paragraphs whose raw line starts with 1-3 literal spaces (not
   * enough to reclassify as an indented code block) get a native HyperMD
   * "hang" from Obsidian: a `padding-inline-start`/`text-indent` pair meant
   * to keep soft-wrapped continuation lines aligned under the first visible
   * character. Our own `padding-left` above always wins that fight (`!important`
   * beats a non-important inline style even across the logical/physical
   * property pair, confirmed live) — but `text-indent` is never touched by
   * us at all, so its native negative value (which Obsidian derives from a
   * measurement taken AFTER our own padding has already shifted the box,
   * confirmed live: for a single leading space the observed value wasn't
   * ~4px, the width of one space, but ~4px + our own padding-left, i.e. it
   * double-counts our own contribution) leaks straight through unopposed.
   * Net first-line shift becomes `ourPadding - nativeTextIndent`, which is
   * NEGATIVE — outdented past the depth column, growing with every extra
   * leading space (more native "measured" width to subtract), exactly the
   * reported bug. Zeroing text-indent removes the hang outright: the line
   * renders purely at our own depth position, and the literal leading
   * spaces still show up as ordinary rendered content on top of it (additive
   * -only, same invariant every other kind here already keeps) instead of
   * being folded into a hanging-indent calculation that assumes zero prior
   * padding. */
  text-indent: 0 !important;
}

/* Atoms (code/table/quote/callout/html/hr) render a visible background or
 * border box; padding-left only shifts an element's own content, never
 * that box, so atoms need margin-left instead. */
.markdown-source-view.mod-cm6 .cm-content > .cm-line.to-decor-atom {
  position: relative;
  margin-left: calc(
    var(--to-depth, 0) * var(--to-decor-unit) + var(--to-marker-gutter, 0px)
  ) !important;
}

/* List items: the SUPPLEMENTAL depth, the distance from the document root down
 * to the list's own root. `margin-left` is a box-model property native list
 * rendering does not otherwise use, so this contribution is additive on top of
 * whatever positions the item within its own list — it moves the line box and
 * nothing inside it.

 * What happens inside the line box is the list-grid section's business, and it

 * is why they are separate rules — this one holds even with every rule below

 * A list line reserves no gutter of its own — its native marker already

 * set on the line (`lineDecoration`), because the marker-column rules below
 * size the marker span to it and a fallback literal here would be a second copy
 * of `MARKER_GUTTER_CSS` to keep in step by hand. */

  margin-left: calc(var(--to-supp-depth, 0) * var(--to-decor-unit)) !important;

 * hangs off `to-decor-list`, a class the decoration puts on LIST-ITEM LINES
 * ONLY, so both gates — outline mode, and "lists only" — come from the

 * What this does NOT get for free is the hanging indent; see `--to-list-hang`

  --list-indent: var(--to-decor-unit);

   * default — measured against the block icons' ink, which are 0.85rem at
   * stroke-width 1.5 in this same `--text-faint`. */
  --list-bullet-size: 0.38em;

/**
 * The outline's visual vocabulary, in one place, for every surface that draws
 * it.
 *
 * Until the backlinks footer there was only one surface, so these values lived
 * inside `decorations.ts` next to their only consumer. A second surface makes
 * that a latent divergence: two renderers each holding their own copy of "how
 * wide is one level of indentation" agree only until someone changes one of
 * them. The editor keeps its own line-decoration machinery; what it shares with
 * the footer is this — the numbers and the custom-property names.
 *
 * Geometry is expressed in `rem` so it tracks the reader's font size, and as
 * `var(--name, fallback)` expressions so a theme or snippet can retune the
 * whole outline without a plugin setting and without either surface knowing.
 *
 * NOTE on fallbacks: `--to-decor-unit` is DECLARED in styles.css, so the
 * expressions here read it without one. A literal fallback would be a second
 * copy of the number living in JS, and the two would eventually disagree —
 * the same reasoning `decorations.ts` records at its own `UNIT`, one level up.
 *
 * The unit goes further than that: this module holds NO form of its value, not
 * even an unused one. Overriding the single declaration is the supported way to
 * retune the outline's width, and that guarantee is only as good as the absence
 * of second copies — a number cannot follow an override, so the first caller to
 * position something from one would leave that piece behind on the old grid
 * while every other layer moved. `UNIT_EXPR` is the only way to refer to it.
 */

/**
 * The visual gap between a mark's ink and the text that mark names.
 *
 * The one value in the gutter's derivation that is chosen rather than measured.
 * Its floor is not free: every mark whose row is written with a single space
 * after it is sized as "the gutter, less one space", so a gap under a space's
 * own advance drives that sizing negative and the mark overflows into the column
 * its text was to begin on. A space's advance varies with the reader's font,
 * which is why this sits clear of it rather than on it.
 *
 * Argued once, in docs/research/21-marker-text-gap.md.
 */
export const MARKER_GAP_REM = 0.375;

/**
 * The ink the gutter reserves whatever the theme does — a floor, not the answer.
 *
 * It covers the marks this layer draws for itself, which are much narrower than
 * this (an icon's glyph, a bullet's dot), and it is set well above them for a
 * second reason: a single-digit ordered number's own box is sized "gutter less
 * one space", so a gutter that collapsed to the icon's width would push an
 * ordered item's text off the column its siblings share.
 *
 * A checkbox is not covered here, because it is not ours to predict — see the
 * expression below.
 */
export const MIN_MARK_INK_REM = 0.5;

/** The marker glyph's own box. */
export const MARKER_ICON_REM = 0.85;

/**
 * Horizontal room reserved for a block marker, left of a node's content.
 *
 * DERIVED, and derived AT RENDER TIME rather than frozen into a number here.
 *
 * The widest mark this layer positions is a task's checkbox, and its size is the
 * theme's — `--checkbox-size`, which Obsidian resolves differently per platform
 * (measured: 16px on desktop, 18.4px on mobile). A constant taken from one of
 * them is wrong on the other, and wrong in the quiet way this whole derivation
 * exists to prevent: the checkbox does not clip, its own text simply leaves the
 * column every other kind's text sits on. So the checkbox term reads the live
 * value and the arithmetic happens in CSS.

 * complaining.

  markerGutter: '--to-marker-gutter',
  markerGap: '--to-marker-gap',

This is a goldmine — the markerX value of 15.62 on macOS for a depth-0 list item likely differs slightly on CI's Linux font, maybe around 14.88, since glyph and bullet padding vary by font. This confirms the hypothesis: the whole document was undecorated because outline mode was off, or the decoration returned none.

I also notice something interesting: in mode=on there are two rows mapping to n=5 — the backlinks footer and the actual last line — so looking up row 5 would grab the footer instead, though that's not what's causing this particular failure. Now I want to trace why outline mode ends up off in the first place, so I'm tracing through the note-opening and toggle-outline-mode logic to see how the mode gets determined and set for a newly created note.

After the toggle persists and fires a notice, it calls `refreshDecorations` and then forces a cursor dispatch to make the ViewPlugin recompute — but I'm wondering whether setting the cursor to its same position actually triggers a real CM6 transaction, and whether a transaction filter in this plugin might be intercepting or cancelling that dispatch before the decorations get a chance to update.

But that would be a consistent failure, not an intermittent one. The more likely culprit for flakiness is the async save: since the toggle command doesn't await the save before firing the notice and refresh, if `saveData` is slow under CI load (multiple Electron instances competing for disk), the refresh could happen well after the test's measurement window closes.

Let me trace what `dismissNotices()` actually waits for, and check the registry's toggle logic more closely. I also want to reconsider the sequence of tests — the one right before this that opens a note with mode 'off' shouldn't trigger a toggle at all, since a brand-new note's outline state already matches 'off'.

I think I've found it: each iteration's toggle flips the in-memory set synchronously, but the actual save is delayed 900ms. So when a previous iteration's save resolves during a later iteration, its nudge dispatch recomputes the view and accidentally decorates the current note early — a stale toggle rescuing the next one. That's the source of the flakiness: it's not deterministic, it's this accidental masking effect, which explains why CI only sometimes catches it and why later screenshots show a decorated document.

For the fix, I need to decouple visible redraws from the awaited disk write. Right now the registry flips state in memory, then awaits a save, and only after that does the plugin nudge the editor to force CM6 to recompute decorations — meaning the outline's appearance is gated on disk latency, and the test's fixed-delay wait is essentially gambling against that write. The fix needs two parts: first, making the redraw depend on the synchronous in-memory flip rather than the completed save, which means restructuring toggle to expose the new state immediately while the persistence continues separately.

I'm considering having the toggle method mutate its internal state before the first await, then return the new state synchronously along with a separate promise for the save, so the notice, footer refresh, and decoration refresh can all happen right away without waiting for the write to finish, and only await the save at the very end for callers that need to know it completed. This depends on the mutation happening before any await inside the registry's toggle implementation.

But that changes every call site, so let me check how many places actually call `registry.toggle` — I see it used in main.ts for toggleMode and forceRedraw, plus the tests. Before committing to that redesign, I should step back and question whether this is really the right fix at all: the actual cause is that the plugin gates the redraw on a disk write, which is a genuine, user-visible latency worth addressing.

The real fix should attack both sides: the product shouldn't block redraw on disk I/O, and the test's `toggleOutlineMode()` should wait for the observable effect instead of relying on a fixed sleep. If the redraw becomes synchronous within command dispatch, `runCommand` returning would mean the DOM is already updated, making the test's timing gamble moot — that's the strongest fix, though making the helper explicitly wait is cheap insurance across all 83 call sites. I'm now weighing whether the helper change is even necessary once the product fix makes things synchronous, since `executeCommandById` would run `toggleMode` synchronously up to its first await.

---
name: comments-explain-not-advocate
description: "Code and workflow comments must not carry measurements, sales pitches, or restatements of the code"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
---

Comments in committed code, workflows, and config must explain what is not visible from the code and will not expire. Three things must stay out: point-in-time data (timing tables, speedup ratios, observed flake rates, run counts, file counts, lists of which files currently do X), advocacy for the change being made, and restatements of the line below.

**Why:** Data-driven decisions are good; embedding the data in a comment is not. A benchmark table is true when written and silently wrong after the next runner image, dependency bump, or tuning pass, and a comment that has quietly become false is worse than no comment. Advocacy ("Measured, not picked", "earned its keep", "this is safe because I verified…") is writing aimed at a reviewer of the current PR, not a reader of the code a year on. See also [[docs-neutral-team-voice]].

**How to apply:** Before committing, reread every comment added and cut anything that (a) contains a number that could change, (b) names specific files/specs as an exhaustive list, (c) argues the change was correct, or (d) paraphrases the code. Keep only mechanics a reader could break by accident — hidden coupling between settings, non-obvious tool behavior (`shell: bash` runs under `-e`), which guarantee actually holds versus which is a convention. Measurements belong in the PR description or commit message, which are dated records, not living documentation. Delete scaffolding rather than keeping it "in case" — unexercised workflows and dead config rot invisibly.

python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path('src/plugin/mode-registry.ts')
s = p.read_text()
old_start = s.index("  /**\n   * Flips `path`'s mode")
old_end = s.index("  async handleRename")
new = """  /**
   * Flips `path`'s mode and reports the state in force from here on, with the
   * write that records it still in flight.
   *
   * Synchronous in what it decides, asynchronous only in what it stores. The
   * mode IS this object's own `Set`; `data.json` is where that set survives a
   * restart, and no reader of the mode consults the file. Reporting the new
   * state only once the write resolved put every visible consequence of a
   * toggle behind disk latency, which is a real wait rather than a theoretical
   * one: a mode change dispatches no CM6 transaction of its own, so the editor
   * repaints only when the plugin nudges it, and that nudge waited on the
   * write.
   *
   * `saved` is handed back rather than dropped, so a caller that genuinely
   * needs the file on disk can still wait for it, and a failed write still
   * reaches whoever asked for the toggle.
   */
  toggle(path: string): { on: boolean; saved: Promise<void> } {
    const on = !this.paths.has(path);
    if (on) this.paths.add(path);
    else this.paths.delete(path);
    return { on, saved: this.save() };
  }

"""
p.write_text(s[:old_start] + new + s[old_end:])
print('ok')
PY

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path('docs/research/11-decoration-lessons.md')
s = p.read_text()
entry = """
- **An intermittent e2e failure whose signature is "no decoration at all" points at the mode
  toggle, not at the geometry the assertion is about.** `56-list-grid.e2e.ts`'s space-indent
  case failed on CI with the depth-0 column expected and a marker ~15px right of it. That
  number is not a geometry error: it is where Obsidian's own native bullet sits on an
  undecorated list line, and the line's `--to-depth` was absent entirely, so `column` read 0
  for a line whose real depth was 1. Measuring the undecorated note directly (mode off,
  `markerX` 15.62px on macOS against the 14.88px CI reported) is what identified the state in
  one step, and it is worth doing first whenever a decoration assertion reports a value near a
  native one.

  The cause was in the plugin, not the spec. A mode toggle dispatches no CM6 transaction of
  its own, so the decorations recompute only when `refreshDecorations` nudges the cursor — and
  `toggleMode` awaited `registry.toggle`, which awaited `saveData`, before reaching that nudge.
  Every visible consequence of the toggle therefore sat behind a `data.json` write. Under load
  a single `saveData` was measured at up to 754ms on a fast machine, against the ~500ms of
  fixed pauses the spec's `open()` spends before measuring. Reproduced exactly by slowing the
  write to 900ms: the first note came back with no `--to-depth` and the native marker column.
  `OutlineModeRegistry.toggle` now decides synchronously and returns the write still in
  flight, so the paint happens in the command's own turn; `10-outline-mode.e2e.ts` pins that by
  reading the DOM in the same synchronous turn as `executeCommandById`, which no amount of
  waiting can make pass on the old code.

  Two things about it made the failure rare rather than deterministic. A pending toggle's
  `nudgeFooters` dispatch lands on whatever note is open when the write finally resolves, so a
  slow toggle silently repaints the NEXT note — which is why only one of five consecutive
  notes reproduced under an injected delay. And the failure screenshot, captured a couple of
  WebDriver round trips after the assertion, shows the note correctly decorated: the paint had
  arrived by then, which reads as "the assertion was wrong" rather than "the paint was late".

- **`requestAnimationFrame` is the wrong instrument for measuring how long a DOM effect took.**
  Polling for the decoration with rAF reported 282–1890ms under machine load; a
  `MutationObserver` on the same mutation, in the same run, reported 30–62ms. Frame callbacks
  are throttled by exactly the contention being investigated, so an rAF-based latency figure
  mostly measures the scheduler. Had the first number been believed, the search would have
  stopped at "the toggle is slow" with a plausible-looking and wrong mechanism.
"""
assert s.endswith('\n')
p.write_text(s + entry)
print('ok')
PY
tail -5 docs/research/11-decoration-lessons.md

17:### Requirement: Mode persistence in plugin data
--- head ---
# outline-mode Specification

## Purpose
Defines outline mode: a per-note, UI-only toggle that gates access to structural editing
commands without ever modifying note content or metadata, persisted per file path in
plugin data across restarts and renames.
## Requirements
### Requirement: Per-note outline mode toggle
The plugin SHALL provide a command (and editor menu entry) that toggles outline mode for
the active markdown note. The mode SHALL be a pure editor-UI state: toggling it SHALL
never modify the note's content, metadata, or modification time.

#### Scenario: Toggling leaves the file untouched
- **WHEN** outline mode is toggled on and off for a note
- **THEN** the file's bytes and mtime are unchanged at every point

### Requirement: Mode persistence in plugin data
Outline mode state SHALL be remembered per note in the plugin data store (keyed by file
path), surviving app restarts. It SHALL never be written into the note (no frontmatter,
no markers). Renamed files SHALL keep their mode; deleted files SHALL be pruned from the
store.

#### Scenario: Mode survives restart
- **WHEN** outline mode is enabled for a note and Obsidian is restarted
- **THEN** the note reopens with outline mode enabled, and the note's content contains no
  trace of the mode

#### Scenario: Rename migrates state
- **WHEN** a note with outline mode enabled is renamed within Obsidian
- **THEN** the mode remains enabled under the new path

### Requirement: Mode gates structural commands
Structural editing commands SHALL be available only when the active note has outline mode
enabled (command palette `checkCallback` semantics), and the keyboard grammar SHALL
activate only for files with outline mode enabled. Notes without outline mode SHALL be
completely unaffected by the plugin's editing behavior: palette commands absent and every
grammar key binding declining, leaving stock editor behavior byte-for-byte.

#### Scenario: Commands inactive outside outline mode
- **WHEN** the command palette is opened for a note without outline mode
- **THEN** the structural commands are not offered for that note

#### Scenario: Keyboard grammar inactive outside outline mode
- **WHEN** any grammar-bound key (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Shift+Enter) is
  pressed in a note without outline mode

## Requirements
### Requirement: Per-note outline mode toggle
The plugin SHALL provide a command (and editor menu entry) that toggles outline mode for
the active markdown note. The mode SHALL be a pure editor-UI state: toggling it SHALL
never modify the note's content, metadata, or modification time.

#### Scenario: Toggling leaves the file untouched
- **WHEN** outline mode is toggled on and off for a note
- **THEN** the file's bytes and mtime are unchanged at every point

#### Scenario: The toggle takes effect before it is recorded
- **WHEN** the toggle command runs on a note
- **THEN** the note is rendered in its new mode within that command's own turn,
  with the write that records the mode still in flight

### Requirement: Mode persistence in plugin data
Outline mode state SHALL be remembered per note in the plugin data store (keyed by file
path), surviving app restarts. It SHALL never be written into the note (no frontmatter,
no markers). Renamed files SHALL keep their mode; deleted files SHALL be pruned from the
store.

git commit -F - <<'MSG'
fix(mode): paint a mode toggle before the write that records it

`56-list-grid.e2e.ts`'s space-indent case failed intermittently on CI with a
depth-0 marker sitting ~15px right of its column. That number is not a geometry
error: it is where Obsidian's own native bullet sits on an UNDECORATED list
line, and the line carried no `--to-depth` at all, so the spec read `column` as
0 for a line whose real depth was 1. The whole note was rendering as a stock
note at the moment it was measured.

A mode toggle dispatches no CM6 transaction of its own, so the decorations
recompute only when `refreshDecorations` nudges the cursor — and `toggleMode`
awaited `registry.toggle`, which awaited `saveData`, before reaching that nudge.
Every visible consequence of a toggle therefore sat behind a `data.json` write.
Measured under load on a fast machine, a single `saveData` reached 754ms against
the ~500ms of fixed pauses the spec spends before measuring; reproduced exactly
by slowing the write to 900ms, which produced the CI state on the first note.
Two things kept it rare rather than deterministic: a pending toggle's
`nudgeFooters` dispatch lands on whatever note is open when the write finally
resolves, so a slow toggle silently repaints the NEXT note, and the failure
screenshot — captured a couple of round trips later — shows the note correctly
decorated.

`OutlineModeRegistry.toggle` now decides synchronously and hands back the write
still in flight. `toggleMode` flips the mode, raises the notice, nudges the
footers and repaints before its first yield, then awaits the write last so a
rejected write still surfaces where it did before. `forceRedraw` takes the same
shape: its off/on pair now happens within one turn instead of straddling two
writes, so a settings change no longer renders the note stock in between.

The new e2e case reads the DOM in the same synchronous turn as
`executeCommandById`, which no amount of waiting can make pass on the old code —
confirmed by reverting the fix. Full desktop suite green.

Docs: the diagnosis in docs/research/11, including that rAF is the wrong
instrument for this measurement (282-1890ms by rAF polling against 30-62ms by
MutationObserver, same run); the settings setters, which still have the old
shape, parked in docs/research/12.
MSG
